title: Samples bakehouse Use Cases Catalog
executive_summary:
Samples bakehouse operates in a business where margins are shaped daily by what comes out of the oven, what sells before close, and how customers feel about every visit. This catalog positions Samples bakehouse to turn its operational, sales, and customer-voice data into a durable competitive advantage, moving from intuition-led decisions to evidence-led ones across production, pricing, and franchise execution.

Concrete opportunities make this tangible. Forecast Product Demand to Reduce Waste lets production planners right-size next-day batches so unsold quantity waste shrinks while recovering lost sales. Reduce Customer Attrition to Protect Revenue gives retention teams a ranked queue of at-risk customers to defend spend before it lapses. Detect Shifting Customer Concerns to Lower Risk surfaces emerging themes across review periods before they harden into reputation damage.

With Databricks Genie Code, Samples bakehouse can unlock these outcomes without heavy engineering overhead, letting business owners query data in plain language, operationalize forecasts, and act on customer sentiment at the pace a bakery and franchise network demands. The result is a measurable lift in revenue protection, margin recovery, and brand strength.

domains.summary:
The Menu domain is where Samples bakehouse converts baking craft into profitable, waste-aware assortment decisions. It governs what is produced, how it is bundled, and how local tastes shape each counter, making it central to both margin and customer satisfaction.

Forecast Product Demand to Reduce Waste equips production planners to adjust next-day batch sizes per product, cutting unsold quantity waste while recovering lost sales. Increase Basket Size to Grow Revenue arms merchandising managers with bundle and counter-prompt offers that lift average totalPrice and quantity per transaction. Optimize Local Product Mix to Grow Revenue tailors assortment plans per location to match regional demand.

With Databricks Genie Code, these decisions become fast and repeatable, letting teams forecast, test bundles, and refine local mix directly from their data to grow revenue and shrink waste at the same time.

use_cases.Name: Forecast Daily Product Demand with Production Planning Recommendations
use_cases.usecase: Forecast Product Demand to Reduce Waste
use_cases.Statement: Perishable baked goods lose value fast, and without a per-product demand forecast the production team over-bakes some items and under-bakes others, driving both waste and lost sales recorded in `quantity` and `totalPrice`.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code aggregates `quantity` by `product` and day from `dateTime`, fits a per-product time-series forecast, then uses ai_query to translate forecasts into daily batch-size recommendations.
use_cases.Business Value: The Production Planner adjusts next-day batch sizes per product, reducing unsold `quantity` waste and recovering sales lost to stockouts [ESTIMATE: depends on `quantity`, `totalPrice`].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: dateTime, product, quantity. Aggregate quantity sold per product per day from dateTime, build calendar features (day-of-week, month), fit a per-product Prophet or ai_forecast model to project next-7-day demand, then use ai_query to convert the forecasts into product-level batch-size recommendations for the baking schedule.
use_cases.Strategic Goals Alignment: Reduce Cost, Boost Productivity, Increase Revenue, Enable Data-Driven Decisions
use_cases.Justification: Per-product demand forecasts directly reduce perishable waste and recover stockout sales, hitting both cost and revenue lines computable from quantity and totalPrice.
use_cases.Quality Summary: `quantity` is summed per `product` per day from `dateTime`, enriched with calendar features (day-of-week, month) and fit with per-product Prophet or ai_forecast to project next-7-day demand. The forecasted demand KPI is converted by ai_query into batch-size recommendations, directly cutting unsold `quantity` waste and recovering stockout sales in `totalPrice` [ESTIMATE: depends on `quantity`, `totalPrice`].
use_cases.bob_justification: `quantity` by `product`/day from `dateTime` forecasts batch sizes, directly cutting perishable waste; weakest D17 (per-product forecast errors need explanation).

use_cases.genie_instruction:
## 1. Decision and Owner

This notebook changes the next-day per-product baking batch sizes: the Production Planner uses the forecast to decide how much of each product to bake so that unsold `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.quantity` waste and stockout losses both fall. The decision owner is the Production Planner (sponsored by the Chief Operating Officer); the cadence is daily, aligned to the next-7-day production schedule. The KPI is forecast accuracy measured as MASE against the seasonal naive forecast, where lower is better, in service of reduced unsold `quantity` and recovered sales recorded in `samples.bakehouse.totalPrice`. The ranked daily batch-size recommendations go to the Production Planner. Decision owner, cadence, KPI and value tier were "not assessed" in the DECISION BLOCK, so the roles stated here come only from the Beneficiary and Sponsor fields; no team size or numeric target is invented.

## 2. Data Plan

There is one table, `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`, acting as the event-fact table; no entity or reference table is needed and no join is performed. The entity key (series key) is `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.product`. The time column is `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.dateTime`, truncated to a calendar date. The measured value per series per day is the sum of `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.quantity`. This is a forecasting (unsupervised, no label) use case, so there is no outcome event rule; the as-of rule is that any forecast or backtest fold trained for a given as-of date uses only rows with `dateTime` strictly before that date (`CAST(dateTime AS DATE) < ctx["as_of_date"]`). The population is all sales rows up to and including the as-of boundary with non-null `product` and non-null `quantity`; filter out rows where `quantity` is null. The other in-scope tables (`samples.bakehouse.media_customer_reviews`, `samples.bakehouse.media_gold_reviews_chunked`) are not used because daily demand per product is fully derivable from the single transactions table.

## 3. Readiness Checks

- `row_count`: count the rows in `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions` with `CAST(dateTime AS DATE) <= ctx["as_of_date"]` and non-null `product` and non-null `quantity`.
- `join_coverage`: this use case reads one table and performs no join, so return 1.0.
- `seasonal_cycles`: compute the span of distinct daily dates (min to max `CAST(dateTime AS DATE)`) up to the as-of date, divide the number of days spanned by SEASON_LENGTH (7), and return that ratio so the gate can confirm at least two weekly cycles exist.
- `staleness_cadences`: compute the number of days (cadences, where one cadence is one day) between the latest `CAST(dateTime AS DATE)` and `ctx["as_of_date"]`; return that count so the gate can confirm the data is at most 2 days stale.
- `missing_period_rate`: across all product series, count the expected (product, day) cells over each series' own observed date range versus the days actually present, and return the share of missing days (expected minus present, divided by expected) as a single pooled rate.

## 4. Slot Tasks

**measure_readiness(ctx)** reads only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. It computes the five keys above and returns the dict `{'row_count', 'join_coverage', 'seasonal_cycles', 'staleness_cadences', 'missing_period_rate'}`. Apply the strictly-before-as-of filter when counting dates for staleness and cycles, and the `<= as_of_date` filter for row_count; do not lower any threshold.

**build_inputs(ctx)** reads only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. Set `SEASON_LENGTH = 7` (weekly seasonality on daily data) and `HORIZON = 7` (the next-7-day production need). Steps: filter to rows with `CAST(dateTime AS DATE) <= ctx["as_of_date"]`, non-null `product`, non-null `quantity`; group by `product` and `CAST(dateTime AS DATE)`; sum `quantity`. Then, per product, build a complete daily calendar from each series' first to last observed day and fill days with no sales as value 0 (a true observed zero-demand day, not fabricated data). The leakage guard: no row with `dateTime` on or after the as-of date enters any series, and no future day is populated. Return a Spark DataFrame with columns `entity_id` (the product string), `period` (DATE), and `value` (the summed daily quantity as a numeric).

**forecast(ctx, history, horizon)** receives a pandas DataFrame `(entity_id, period, value)`. For each `entity_id`, refit from scratch on that series' full history (never persist or register a model), using statsmodels ExponentialSmoothing with a weekly seasonal period of 7 when the series has at least two full weekly cycles, otherwise fall back to the seasonal naive value (the value 7 periods earlier). Produce the next `horizon` daily periods after each series' last `period`. Clip forecasts at 0 (demand cannot be negative) and round to whole units since batches are counts. Return a pandas DataFrame with columns `entity_id`, `period` (the next `horizon` dates per series), and `forecast`.

**OUTPUT_COLUMNS mapping** sets `entity_label` to the product name so the Production Planner reads a per-product label; `VALUE_TYPE` stays `'forecast'`. No source table is read here beyond what Inspire's writer supplies.

## 5. Method and Baseline

The candidate method is statsmodels ExponentialSmoothing (Holt-Winters) with weekly seasonality (period 7) per product series, the simplest method that can beat the baseline; for very short series it degrades to the seasonal naive value. The baseline Inspire fits is the seasonal naive forecast (the value one 7-day season earlier). Acceptance rule in plain words: Inspire runs a rolling-origin backtest with at least 3 folds; if the candidate's MASE is below 1.0 against the seasonal naive forecast, the candidate is published, otherwise Inspire publishes the seasonal naive forecast flagged as the fallback. Data risks are handled as follows: weekly seasonality is modeled by the period-7 seasonal term; missing periods are filled with observed zeros so demand gaps are not treated as unknowns; sparse or very short series automatically fall back to seasonal naive; there is no class imbalance (this is numeric forecasting) and no free text, so no text-quality handling is needed. This execution pattern (family E) registers no model and makes no extra `ai_query` call in the slots; Inspire's own explanation and summary cells handle any AI narration on the top rows.

## 6. Output Mapping

Genie Code maps `entity_label` to `product`. The `value` column carries the forecast daily demand in whole units of `quantity` (units of product per day), which the Production Planner reads directly as the recommended batch size for that day. `segment_or_item` carries the forecast `period` (the target day within the next-7-day horizon) so each product has one row per forecast day. Each row's top reasons are rule-based and derived from the series' own recent pattern: the day-of-week level and the trend direction relative to the prior week (for example "higher weekend demand" or "declining week-over-week"), stated from the fitted seasonal and trend components, not from an LLM. Set `data_quality_flag` to something other than ok when the series fell back to seasonal naive (too short for Holt-Winters), when the series' `missing_period_rate` is elevated, or when the acceptance backtest failed and the published value is the flagged seasonal naive forecast; otherwise ok. Priority tiers and recommended actions are assigned by Inspire's writer using rules; do not have Genie Code or an LLM set them.

## 7. Definition of Done

- All four GENIE SLOT functions (`measure_readiness`, `build_inputs` with `SEASON_LENGTH`/`HORIZON` set, `forecast`, and the `OUTPUT_COLUMNS`/`VALUE_TYPE` mapping) are filled with the names, arguments and return columns unchanged.
- The notebook ran top to bottom in this session with run controls set to Here, and then again as the tagged job.
- The contract-check cell (the last cell) printed PASSED.
- No Inspire cell was edited, no threshold was changed in code, no table was renamed, no job was created or deleted; only slot cells (and a pinned `%pip install` line if a package is missing) were touched.
- STOP RULE: if the readiness gate raises `InspireReadinessStop` (or `InspireNoChampion`/`InspireRejected`), Genie Code stops, shows the user the plain message the gate printed, and does not lower thresholds, fabricate data, drop a check, switch tables or edit the gate to force a pass.

use_cases.genie_instruction:
## 1. Decision and Owner

This notebook changes which product bundles and counter upsell prompts the Head of Merchandising launches, by turning co-purchase affinity into a ranked list of recommended companion products per anchor product. The decision owner is the Head of Merchandising (sponsored by the Chief Marketing Officer); cadence is not assessed, so treat it as recurring on the run schedule set by the run controls cell. The KPI is average `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.totalPrice` (and `quantity`) per transaction, where higher is better, driven by upsell lift; direction, value tier and target are not assessed, so state no numeric target. The ranked top-K output goes to the Head of Merchandising for bundle and counter-prompt offers.

## 2. Data Plan

There is one table, `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`, which serves as the event-fact table; no join is needed, so the join path is a single table and join coverage is 1.0. The basket (entity) key is `sales_transactions.transactionID`; the item is `sales_transactions.product`; the time column is `sales_transactions.dateTime`. This is an unsupervised affinity and recommendation use case (Recommendation, family D), so there is no supervised outcome rule: the "interaction" is a product appearing in a transaction basket. Apply the as-of rule strictly: `build_inputs` and `measure_readiness` read only rows where `sales_transactions.dateTime` is strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`. Population filters: keep rows with non-null `transactionID` and non-null `product`; drop rows with non-positive `quantity` when `quantity` is present so a line item represents a real purchase. Do not use `samples.bakehouse.media_customer_reviews` or `media_gold_reviews_chunked`: the plan works on the single primary table and needs no review text.

## 3. Readiness Checks

- `row_count`: count rows in `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions` where `dateTime` is strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]` after the population filters.
- `join_coverage`: return 1.0, because this use case reads one table and there is no join path.
- `interactions`: count the retained line-item rows (one per `transactionID`, `product` occurrence) before `as_of_date`; this is the number of basket-item interactions.
- `users`: count distinct `sales_transactions.transactionID` (the recommender entity is the basket) over the retained rows before `as_of_date`.
- `items`: count distinct `sales_transactions.product` over the retained rows before `as_of_date`.

## 4. Slot Tasks

`measure_readiness(ctx)` reads only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. It applies the as-of filter (`dateTime` < `ctx["as_of_date"]`) and the population filters, then returns the dict with `row_count`, `join_coverage` (1.0), `interactions`, `users` and `items` computed as in Section 3. Return plain Python numbers.

`build_inputs(ctx, as_of_date)` reads only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. Filter to rows with `dateTime` strictly before `as_of_date` (the leakage guard: never read on-or-after rows), non-null `transactionID` and `product`, and `quantity` positive when present. Return a Spark DataFrame with exactly these columns: `entity_id` = `transactionID`, `item_id` = `product`, `weight` = the summed `quantity` for that `transactionID`/`product` (use 1 where `quantity` is null), and `event_time` = the row's `dateTime` (use the max `dateTime` per basket-item if aggregated).

`fit_candidates(ctx, interactions)` takes the pandas DataFrame from `build_inputs`. Build a sparse basket-by-item matrix (rows = `entity_id`, columns = `item_id`, values = `weight`) with scipy, then fit item-item cosine similarity with scikit-learn. Return `{"item_item_cosine": fitted_object}` holding the item index and the item-item similarity matrix.

`predict(ctx, model, entities, k)` takes a pandas DataFrame of `entity_id`. For each entity, score candidate items as the weighted sum of similarities to the items that entity already holds, exclude any `item_id` the entity already interacted with, and keep the top `k`. Return a pandas DataFrame with exactly `entity_id`, `item_id`, `score`.

## 5. Method and Baseline

Use item-item cosine similarity on the sparse basket-item interaction matrix (scikit-learn plus scipy sparse); this is the simplest method that can beat popularity and stays well under the serverless model-size limit. The baseline Inspire fits is the most popular items. Acceptance: the challenger is promoted to champion only when its out-of-time precision@K is at least 1.1 times the popularity baseline's precision@K; otherwise it stays challenger and the current champion is kept. Handle this data's risks: sparse anchors are protected by the readiness floors (>= 1000 interactions, >= 100 baskets, >= 100 products), so if the data is too thin the gate stops the run; seasonality and missing periods are handled by the strict as-of split so training uses only past baskets and evaluation is out-of-time; always exclude items already in the basket to avoid trivial self-recommendations. No AI function is called in these slots; Inspire's explanation and summary cells already run `ai_query` on the top rows, so add no other AI calls.

## 6. Output Mapping

Map `entity_label` to the anchor `sales_transactions.product` (the item for which companions are recommended); keep `OUTPUT_COLUMNS` with `entity_label` as given and `VALUE_TYPE = 'recommendation score'`. `value` is the recommendation score from `predict` (the cosine-weighted affinity score, unitless and ranked, not a currency amount). `segment_or_item` carries the recommended companion `item_id` (the suggested bundle or upsell product). Each row's top reasons come from the association signals between the anchor and the recommended item (co-occurrence support, confidence and lift computed from the baskets), expressed as rule-based reasons, not model internals. Set `data_quality_flag` to other than ok when the anchor product has very few supporting baskets (thin support) or when `quantity`/`totalPrice` was null and defaulted. Do not ask Genie Code or an LLM to assign priority tiers or recommended actions; Inspire's writer sets those by rule.

## 7. Definition of Done

- All GENIE SLOTS are filled: `measure_readiness`, `build_inputs`, `fit_candidates`, `predict`, and the `OUTPUT_COLUMNS`/`VALUE_TYPE` mapping, each keeping its function names, arguments and return columns.
- The notebook ran top to bottom in this session with run controls set to Here, and then ran as the tagged job.
- The final contract-check cell printed PASSED.
- No Inspire cell was edited, no thresholds were changed in code, the notebook was not renamed, and no job was created or deleted; at most a pinned `%pip install name==version` line was added in the Pinned packages cell if a slot needed a missing package.
- STOP RULE: if the readiness gate raises `InspireReadinessStop`, `InspireNoChampion` or `InspireRejected`, Genie Code must stop, show the user the plain message the gate printed, and must not lower thresholds, fabricate data, drop a check, switch tables or edit the gate to force a pass.

use_cases.Name: Optimize Product Mix by Franchise with Localized Menu Assortment Plan
use_cases.usecase: Optimize Local Product Mix to Grow Revenue
use_cases.Statement: A one-size-fits-all menu ignores that different franchises sell different products in different proportions, leaving revenue on the table where local demand is misaligned with the offered mix.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code computes per-franchise product revenue and quantity contribution and solves a constrained assortment optimization that reallocates emphasis toward locally high-performing `product` lines subject to a limited menu-slot constraint.
use_cases.Business Value: The Franchise Operations Director receives a per-location menu assortment plan, aiming to grow `totalPrice` by aligning the product mix with local demand revealed in `quantity` and `product` patterns [ESTIMATE: depends on `totalPrice`].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: franchiseID, product, quantity, totalPrice, dateTime. Compute per-franchise product-level revenue and velocity, formulate a constrained optimization that maximizes expected revenue subject to a fixed menu-slot count per franchise, generate recommended keep/add/drop assortments, then use ai_query to explain each recommendation and localize the menu plan.
use_cases.Strategic Goals Alignment: Increase Revenue, Enable Data-Driven Decisions
use_cases.Justification: Constrained assortment optimization per franchise aligns menu to local demand to grow totalPrice; distinct optimization question from momentum classification.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Per-`franchiseID` product-level revenue and velocity from `quantity`, `totalPrice`, `dateTime` feed a constrained optimization maximizing expected revenue under a fixed menu-slot count, yielding keep/add/drop assortments. ai_query localizes each plan, directly targeting `totalPrice` growth from demand-aligned mix [ESTIMATE: depends on `totalPrice`].
use_cases.bob_justification: Per-`franchiseID` `product` velocity feeds a slot-constrained assortment optimization on `totalPrice`; weakest D17 (optimization output less transparent).

domains.summary:

use_cases.genie_instruction:
## 1. Decision and Owner

This notebook changes whether and when the retention team proactively reaches out to a repeat customer who is quietly lapsing, by producing a ranked queue of at-risk customers scored by lapse probability. The decision owner is the Head of Customer Retention (the Beneficiary), sponsored by the Chief Marketing Officer; cadence is not assessed in the DECISION BLOCK, so the queue is refreshed on each scoring run. The KPI is lapse rate and recovered recurring spend tracked in `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.totalPrice`, where lower lapse rate and higher recovered spend count as better [ESTIMATE: depends on `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.customerID`, `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.totalPrice`]. The ranked output goes to the Head of Customer Retention.

## 2. Data Plan

There is one table, `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`, acting as both the event facts and the entity source; no join is needed, so join coverage is 1.0 and no reference or enrichment table is used (the review tables add nothing to purchase-interval and spend-trend features). The entity key is `sales_transactions.customerID`. The time column is `sales_transactions.dateTime`. As-of rule: every feature for an as_of_date uses only transactions with `sales_transactions.dateTime` strictly before that as_of_date. Outcome rule (churn / lapse): for a customer who was active on or before an as_of_date, the label is 1 when that customer has no transaction (no row in `sales_transactions`) in the window `(as_of_date, as_of_date + OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS]`, else 0. Open cases are excluded: a customer is scored or labeled only when the full outcome window has closed on or before the data's maximum `dateTime` (training), and at scoring time only customers whose window is still open on `ctx["as_of_date"]` are returned. Population filter: customers with at least two prior purchases before the as_of_date (repeat customers), since one-time buyers have no inter-purchase interval to model.

## 3. Readiness Checks

- `row_count`: count all rows in `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions` with `dateTime` on or before `ctx["as_of_date"]`.
- `join_coverage`: single table, no join path, so return 1.0.
- `outcome_derivable`: True when `dateTime`, `customerID` and `totalPrice` are non-null on enough rows to build at least one closed outcome window and derive repeat-customer labels; else False.
- `positives`: count of customer-plus-as_of_date rows across the closed training windows whose label equals 1 (lapsed within the window), computed by the same no-purchase rule in Section 2.
- `class_rate`: positives divided by the total labeled customer-window rows across the closed training windows.
- `outcome_windows`: the number of distinct closed outcome windows of length OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS that fit entirely within the observed `dateTime` span up to `ctx["as_of_date"]`.

## 4. Slot Tasks

**measure_readiness(ctx):** Read only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. Compute the six keys exactly as in Section 3 as of `ctx["as_of_date"]`, deriving labels for the repeat-customer population under the no-purchase rule, and return the dict with keys `row_count`, `join_coverage`, `outcome_derivable`, `positives`, `class_rate`, `outcome_windows`. Do not change thresholds.

**build_inputs(ctx, as_of_dates, scoring=False):** Set `OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS` from the outcome definition; given no assessed window, use 90 days (a trailing lapse window) and keep `TRAINING_WINDOWS = 6`. Read `ctx["source_tables"]` when training and `ctx["scoring_tables"]` when scoring (both resolve to `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`). For each `customerID` and each as_of_date, using only rows with `dateTime` strictly before that as_of_date (leakage guard), derive numeric features: mean and standard deviation of inter-purchase gap in days, days since last purchase, tenure in days (first to last prior purchase), total and recent-window purchase count, mean `totalPrice`, trailing spend trend (recent-period vs earlier-period mean `totalPrice`), total `quantity` and mean `quantity`. Restrict to the repeat-customer population (>= 2 prior purchases). Return `entity_id` (customerID), `as_of_date` (DATE), the numeric feature columns, and an `entity_label` text column (for example a string built from customerID). With `scoring=True`, return only customers whose outcome window is still open on `ctx["as_of_date"]`.

**build_label(ctx, as_of_dates):** Read `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. For each `customerID` and as_of_date in the training population, return `entity_id`, `as_of_date`, and `label` = 1 when the customer has no transaction in `(as_of_date, as_of_date + OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS]`, else 0, excluding any as_of_date whose window has not fully closed in the data.

**fit_candidates(ctx, X_train, y_train):** Set `BASELINE_FEATURES` to the strongest signals (days since last purchase, mean inter-purchase gap, spend trend). Return a dict of one or two scikit-learn estimators, primarily a `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` with class weighting for imbalance; no deep learning.

**predict(ctx, model, X):** Return one lapse probability per row of X (the churn risk score).

**explanation_inputs(ctx, model, X):** Return None to use Inspire's rule-based reasons.

## 5. Method and Baseline

The candidate method is a scikit-learn `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` on the as-of features, with class weights to handle imbalance; the simpler fallback candidate is a balanced logistic regression on `BASELINE_FEATURES`. Inspire's baseline is the class rate plus a balanced logistic regression on the strongest signals. Acceptance: on the most recent closed outcome window using a time-aware split, out-of-time AUC must be at least 0.6, PR-AUC at least 1.5 times the class rate, and AUC at least 0.02 above the baseline. Class imbalance is handled by class weights and the PR-AUC-lift gate; seasonality and missing periods are handled by using rolling trailing windows and days-since-last-purchase rather than fixed calendar features; sparse entities are excluded by the repeat-customer filter (>= 2 prior purchases); no text model is used, so review text quality is not a factor. The only AI function call is Inspire's own `ai_query` in the explanation and summary cells; the slots add no `ai_query` calls.

## 6. Output Mapping

Map `entity_label` to the `entity_label` text column built in `build_inputs` from `customerID`. `value` is the lapse probability (`VALUE_TYPE = 'probability'`, a 0-to-1 risk score). `segment_or_item` carries the customer identifier (`customerID`). Each row's top reasons come from Inspire's rule-based reasons (`explanation_inputs` returns None), surfacing the most unusual feature values such as elevated days-since-last-purchase or a declining spend trend. Set `data_quality_flag` to something other than ok when a customer has very few prior purchases near the repeat threshold, a missing or null `totalPrice` history, or an inter-purchase gap undefined. Priority tiers and recommended actions are assigned by Inspire's writer rules; do not have Genie Code or an LLM assign them.

## 7. Definition of Done

- Every GENIE SLOT (`measure_readiness`, `build_inputs`, `build_label`, `fit_candidates`, `predict`, `explanation_inputs`, `OUTPUT_COLUMNS`/`VALUE_TYPE`) is filled with its exact function names, arguments and return columns intact.

The ranked output goes to the Head of Customer Marketing.

## 2. Data Plan

Use one table, `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`, as the event-fact and entity source; no join is needed, so join coverage is 1.0 and no OTHER TABLES IN SCOPE are required for this plan. The entity key is `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.customerID` and the time column is `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.dateTime`. The as-of rule: every feature for `ctx["as_of_date"]` uses only transactions with `dateTime` strictly before that date; the "reference" window is a trailing baseline period ending strictly before the current window, and the "current" window is the most recent scored period ending at the as-of date. This is an unsupervised anomaly use case, so there is no outcome label and no open-case exclusion. The population the decision acts on is high-value customers: aggregate `totalPrice` per `customerID` over the reference window and keep only customers whose cumulative reference spend ranks in the top band (for example the top spend quantile), because the business targets concentrated revenue at risk; filter out rows with null `customerID`, null `dateTime`, or non-positive `totalPrice`.

## 3. Readiness Checks

- `row_count`: count all rows of `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions` with `dateTime` strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`; threshold is >= 1.
- `join_coverage`: this use case reads one table with no join, so return 1.0.
- `reference_rows`: count rows of `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions` whose `dateTime` falls inside the reference window (strictly before the current window, which itself ends at the as-of date); threshold is >= 1000.
- `key_signal_null_rate`: over rows in the reference window, compute the share of rows where any key signal (`customerID`, `totalPrice`, `quantity`, or `dateTime`) is null or where `totalPrice` is non-positive; threshold is <= 0.2.

## 4. Slot Tasks

`measure_readiness(ctx)` reads only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions` and returns the dict with `row_count`, `join_coverage` (1.0), `reference_rows`, and `key_signal_null_rate` as described in Section 3; it must not apply thresholds itself (the next Inspire cell does).

`build_inputs(ctx, window)` reads only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. For the given window (reference = baseline history strictly before the current window; current = most recent period ending at the as-of date), filter to that window's `dateTime` range, drop null `customerID`/`dateTime` and non-positive `totalPrice`, then aggregate per `customerID` to build behavioral features: recent spend versus trailing baseline (ratio or difference of per-period `totalPrice`), purchase frequency and its decay (count of distinct `transactionID` or transaction days per period), and basket-size change (mean `totalPrice` and mean `quantity` per transaction). Restrict to the high-value population defined in Section 2. Return a Spark DataFrame with `entity_id` set to `customerID`, the numeric signal columns, and optionally `entity_label` (a readable customer identifier derived from `customerID`). Leakage guard: when `window` is "reference", use only `dateTime` strictly before the current window start; both windows must end at or before `ctx["as_of_date"]` and must never read rows dated on or after the as-of date.

`fit_candidates(ctx, X_reference, seed)` fits on the reference feature matrix only and returns `{name: fitted_detector}`, for example `{"isolation_forest": IsolationForest(random_state=seed).fit(X_reference)}` using scikit-learn (no deep learning). `predict(ctx, model, X)` returns one anomaly score per row of `X` with higher meaning more unusual, for example `-model.score_samples(X)`, orienting features so that declining recent spend and frequency produce higher scores. `explanation_inputs(ctx, model, X)` returns None to use Inspire's rule-based reasons.

## 5. Method and Baseline

The candidate method is a scikit-learn `IsolationForest` fit on the reference-window feature matrix and used to score the current window; this is the simplest method that can beat the baseline for multi-feature decline detection. The baseline Inspire fits is a robust z-score rule (median and MAD) on the same signals. Acceptance in plain words: the run keeps at most 200 alerts (top rows by anomaly score at the 0.99 quantile), the top alerts from two fits with different seeds must agree on at least 60 percent of their members, and precision on any known cases must not fall below the baseline. Handle this data's risks by: using per-customer aggregated features so sparse transaction entities do not dominate; using recent-versus-baseline ratios so overall seasonal volume shifts cancel out; dropping customers with too few reference transactions to form a stable baseline rather than imputing fabricated activity; and restricting to the high-value population so the review budget targets concentrated revenue. No AI functions are added in the slots; Inspire's explanation and summary cells already call `ai_query` on the top rows.

## 6. Output Mapping

Map `entity_label` to the readable customer identifier derived from `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.customerID` (or `customerID` itself when no label field is built). `value` is the anomaly score (VALUE_TYPE = 'anomaly score'), a unitless detector score where higher means more anomalous decline; the ranked at-risk-spend ordering is driven by this score combined with the customer's baseline `totalPrice` magnitude in Inspire's writer. `segment_or_item` holds the high-value customer segment context (for example the top-spend band the customer falls into). Each row's top reasons come from Inspire's rule-based reasons (the slot returns None), citing which signal moved most: recent-versus-baseline `totalPrice` drop, frequency decay, or basket-size (`quantity`) change. Set `data_quality_flag` to something other than ok when a scored customer has sparse or borderline reference activity, when any key signal (`totalPrice`, `quantity`, `dateTime`) was null or imputed-away for that customer, or when the current window has unusually thin coverage for that account. Priority tiers and recommended win-back actions are assigned by Inspire's rule-based writer, not by Genie Code or an LLM.

use_cases.genie_instruction:
## 1. Decision and Owner
This notebook changes which products the Head of Pricing corrects when realized price per unit falls systematically below the price the business expects, so that leaked margin is recovered and realized `totalPrice` rises [ESTIMATE: depends on `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.totalPrice`]. The decision owner is the Head of Pricing and the sponsor is the Chief Financial Officer; the DECISION BLOCK lists cadence as not assessed, so treat each run as one analytical refresh that recomputes the findings. The KPI is the effective unit price (`totalPrice` divided by `quantity`), and better means closing the negative gap between realized and expected price (raising realized price toward the modeled expectation). The output is a product-level pricing correction list ranked by systematic negative residual, delivered to the Head of Pricing.

## 2. Data Plan
There is one table, `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`, which plays the role of event facts; it is the primary and only source table, so no join is performed and join coverage is 1.0 by definition. The entity key for findings is `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.product` (the product whose pricing is corrected), computed over individual transactions keyed by `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.transactionID`. The time column is `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.dateTime`. The as-of rule: use only rows with `dateTime` strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`. This is an analytical refresh with no forward-looking label, so there is no outcome-window or open-case exclusion; the computed quantity is observed within each transaction. Population filters: keep rows where `quantity` is greater than 0 (effective unit price divides by `quantity`), where `totalPrice` is greater than 0, and where `product` is not null, so the effective-price computation and the per-product grouping are well defined.

## 3. Readiness Checks
- `row_count`: count rows of `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions` after the population filters (`quantity` > 0, `totalPrice` > 0, `product` not null) and with `dateTime` strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`; threshold >= 1.
- `join_coverage`: this use case reads one table, so return 1.0 (no join path exists); threshold >= 0.8.
- `smallest_group_rows`: group the filtered rows by `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.product` and return the minimum row count across groups that will enter the model; threshold >= 30 rows per group.
- `periods`: count the number of distinct calendar months derived from `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.dateTime` over the filtered rows; threshold >= 2 periods.

## 4. Slot Tasks
`measure_readiness(ctx)` reads only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. It applies the as-of filter (`dateTime` < `ctx["as_of_date"]`) and the population filters, then returns the dict with `row_count`, `join_coverage` (set to 1.0), `smallest_group_rows` (minimum per-`product` count) and `periods` (distinct months of `dateTime`). Return exactly these four keys.

`build_inputs(ctx)` reads only `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions`. It filters to rows with `dateTime` strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]` (the leakage guard: nothing dated on or after the as-of date enters the inputs) and the population filters above, then returns a Spark DataFrame with the columns needed downstream: `transactionID`, `product`, `quantity`, `unitPrice`, `totalPrice`, `dateTime`, and a computed `effective_unit_price` equal to `totalPrice / quantity`.

`analyze(ctx, inputs)` converts the inputs to pandas (the row volume is per-transaction and modest). It fits one Ridge regression of `effective_unit_price` on `product` (one-hot encoded) and `quantity`, standardizing `quantity` before fitting; this yields the expected effective price per transaction. It computes the residual (realized minus expected) per transaction and, for each `product`, the mean residual (the systematic gap). Report one row per `product`: `entity_id` = the product, `segment_or_item` = the product (the dimension corrected), `value` = the mean negative residual effect size in currency per unit, `p_value` = the p-value of a one-sided test that the product's mean residual is below zero (for example a t-test of that product's residuals against zero), and `n` = the number of transactions behind that product. Inspire applies the Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

`OUTPUT_COLUMNS` maps `entity_label` to the product name derived from `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.product`; `VALUE_TYPE` stays `'effect size'`.

## 5. Method and Baseline
The method is Ridge regression (statsmodels or scikit-learn Ridge) of effective unit price on `product` and `quantity`, the simplest regularized linear model that can beat the baseline while damping multicollinearity among correlated product indicators; check VIF on the design before interpreting coefficients. The baseline Inspire fits is the KPI with no drivers: the overall mean effective unit price. Acceptance in plain words: every reported product carries an effect size (its mean residual gap) and survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction at fdr_alpha = 0.05; products whose negative gap is not significant after correction are reported as Monitor only, not corrected. Data risks: sparse products are excluded by the `smallest_group_rows` >= 30 gate so coefficients are stable; seasonality and missing periods are handled by the `periods` >= 2 gate and by reporting effect sizes rather than single-period points; divide-by-zero and bad rows are removed by the `quantity` > 0 and `totalPrice` > 0 filters. Use no random stand-in values. Inspire's explanation and summary cells call `ai_query` on the top rows; the slots add no other AI calls.

## 6. Output Mapping
Genie Code maps `entity_label` to `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions.product` (the product name). The `value` is the effect size: the systematic mean residual gap between realized and expected effective unit price, in currency per unit (negative means realized price sits below expectation). `segment_or_item` holds the product, the dimension the correction acts on. Each row's top reasons are derived from the regression contributions: the product indicator coefficient and the `quantity` effect that together explain the expected price, plus the sign and magnitude of the mean residual. Set `data_quality_flag` to something other than ok when a product's transaction count is near the minimum group threshold, when its residual variance is extreme (unstable estimate), or when a high VIF indicates its coefficient is poorly identified; otherwise ok. Priority tiers and recommended actions are assigned by Inspire's rule-based writer; do not ask Genie Code or an LLM to set them.

## 7. Definition of Done
- All GENIE SLOT functions (`measure_readiness`, `build_inputs`, `analyze`) and the `OUTPUT_COLUMNS`/`VALUE_TYPE` mapping are filled, keeping their names, arguments and return columns.
- `measure_readiness` returns all four keys (`row_count`, `join_coverage`, `smallest_group_rows`, `periods`); `analyze` returns `entity_id`, `segment_or_item`, `value`, `p_value`, `n`.
- The notebook ran top to bottom in this session with run controls set to Here, then ran as the tagged job.
- The contract-check cell (the last cell) printed PASSED.
- No Inspire cell was edited, no thresholds were changed in code, the notebook was not renamed, and only source columns from `samples.bakehouse.sales_transactions` were cited.
- STOP RULE: if the readiness gate raises `InspireReadinessStop` (or `InspireNoChampion`/`InspireRejected`), stop and show the user the plain message the gate printed; do not lower thresholds, fabricate data, drop a check, switch tables or edit the gate to force a pass.

use_cases.usecase: Prevent Fake Review Manipulation to Protect Reputation
use_cases.Statement: Coordinated fake or duplicated reviews distort franchise reputation signals and mislead operational decisions, but near-identical text chunks are not currently flagged for moderation.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code embeds `chunked_text`, clusters chunks with DBSCAN to find dense near-duplicate groups within and across `franchiseID`, then uses ai_query to explain each suspicious cluster and build a moderation investigation queue keyed by `review_uri`.
use_cases.Business Value: The Trust and Safety Lead triages suspected manipulation faster, reducing the count of near-duplicate chunks in `chunked_text` that corrupt reputation metrics tied to `review_uri` [ESTIMATE: depends on `chunked_text`].

use_cases.technique_implementation_guidance:
Method: K-Means or a Gaussian mixture inside a scikit-learn Pipeline with imputation and scaling, choosing the number of segments by silhouette. Use only models that can assign new entities, so segment IDs stay stable between runs.
Baseline: quantile tiers on the most variable feature.
Accept: silhouette, the smallest segment share and bootstrap stability (adjusted Rand index) meet the thresholds.
If data is insufficient: too few entities for the number of segments or fewer than three usable numeric features stop the run at the readiness gate.
